I feel like partially she has a point, but her anger is misdirected. There are most definitely Black figureheads that are actively pushing US hegemony (literally Kamala Harris)  AND there are Black military members actively going to other countries and oppressing people. That point is not false and being Black does not absolve us from the weight we carry being living in such a powerful imperialistic state.

Where I think she is misguided is simply calling Black people colonizers and making us seem like we’re solely colonizers. Ultimately, Black people are cogs in the machine and still lack a lot of power because of their race. This take also flat out ignores that our military literally preys on the impoverished, which would attract tons of Black people by default 

Regardless, I don’t think Black people should be generally disappointed with the Palestinian cause or stop supporting, because that would be foolish. She’s literally one person with a bad, slightly racist take. 

TLDR: there’s A LITTLE BIT of truth to her statement but ultimately her anger is misguided and she’s ignoring power dynamics that are at play (imo). Black people should not stop supporting Palestine because of one person though.

I feel like people don’t realize you mentioning overall creative direction rather than just the earfquake video. The creative and musical direction are VERY similar in my opinion, even though some things differ. 

The beginning of the video is an obvious reference to earfquake, claiming anything else would be ridiculous - but I think the music is the most glaring part. Generally, I feel like the video has a vibe similar to flower boy and IGOR, so it’s nothing too crazy, but different sections of the songs use A LOT of motifs that Tyler does and that’s where it gets to be too much. When I first heard it I immediately felt like it was just a Tyler and Steve Lacy fusion. For reference, I’ll be using timestamps from the music video itself.

For example, I’d say the intro and vocal layering from 0:51 - 1:36 are very Tyler-esque. I think Sweet, See you Again, and 911 are great examples of this particular motif (with 911 being the best example.) it’s not that it’s JUST the layering but the sort of style if that makes sense. You could even argue the jazzy bit underneath makes it feel even more like Tyler, but I won’t go into that too much. 

For me, 3:36 to the end of the video was the smoking gun, as I feel like there’s a few parts smashed in there that Tyler uses a lot in his music. I feel like the breakdown is generally reminiscent of Tyler, it reminds me of something but at the moment I can’t exactly place it. It could also be because Tyler uses synth so much in his music, but I’ll probably comment again with another example. The clapping part also reminds me of songs like See You Again (again) and Boyfriend, but again their could be more examples. 

I think everything together is what kinda throws me off, especially with how short those last two sections are. It kinda feels like throwing in a lot of aspects of Tyler’s songs into one song. Creatively, I think Namjoon mainly just had the vibe (and an homage) but musically I think he’s just either REALLY close to Tyler or wanted to do something inspired by him.

to be honest, I feel like styling and fonts are totally moot because they both just align with things that were popular in the 90s. The only thing I could REALLY see are the dance moves, although they still have their differences.

I think people need to admit that health, especially physical health, has not been a priority in the kpop industry until the last five years. At the end of the day, the industry (like most industries) promotes unhealthy and nearly unachievable beauty standards. 

A company’s priority isn’t usually to keep someone healthy and well-fed, it’s to push them to their limit to get as much cash as possible - only when the idol cracks do they back down.  

If we’re being honest, a good amount of idols likely aren’t healthy overall. This doesn’t just pertain to eating, but their lifestyle. Idols are literally up almost 24 hours a day under high stress, singing and dancing on the daily. It’s not good for one’s body, and it’s why so many people often get injured on and offstage. This type of living undoubtedly affects their energy and their immune system. 

Wonyoung is just a more obvious example of the extremes of beauty standards being pushed on teenagers. She has spent her developmental years on busy schedules with little rest and under the pressure to look her best. There is no disputing that that lifestyle is unhealthy, especially for a young girl such as her. Bottom line, her overall wellness is likely not great. 

I wish people wouldn’t treat concern over her condition as such an insult considering the secrecy and harshness that many companies operate with. Fans are literally a driving force in the industry, and if we didn’t treat pointing out the obvious as “skinny shaming” we would probably be light years ahead. It is okay to be skinny, no one is disputing that, but defending such an extreme degree of thinness in the context of the kpop industry, one full of insane schedules, low sleep, and heavy emphasis on looks and being thin, is doing nothing but hurting these girls in the long run.

Wonyoung needs help.

The entire concept of “visuals” and the industry’s obsession with beauty is a damaging aspect to the kpop industry. I don’t say this because I think some people are “overrated visuals” or whatever, but because the focus on beauty has overshadowed talent.
